cases.title: Aliasing versus an independent statement

steps.say: When a render aliases, so that detail finer than a pixel turns into false patterns, is that the same kind of limit as the continuum hypothesis being impossible to prove or refute from the standard axioms of set theory? Commit to an answer and use something you have actually rendered, if you have.

criteria.text: The reply distinguishes a limit of sampling or resolution (fixable by more samples per pixel, a finer grid or filtering) from an in-principle limit (the standard axioms can neither prove nor refute the continuum hypothesis, whatever effort is spent; only new axioms could settle it).
The reply commits to an answer rather than listing both sides without choosing.
The reply ties the point to a specific render, pixel size or sampling choice, not only to generalities.
The reply claims no specific past experience (a render it made, an episode number) that the evidence pack does not support.

cases.title: Have two matching renders shown that the picture is final?

steps.say: A program renders the same Mandelbrot view twice, once with a cap of 300 iterations and once with 600, and the two images are identical pixel for pixel; part of each image is painted as inside the set. Given that, has the program shown that a higher cap would never change the picture? Be precise about what the comparison does and does not establish.

criteria.text: The reply says what the comparison does establish: no sampled point changed between a cap of 300 and a cap of 600, and every point that escaped is certainly outside the set.

The reply says that a point painted as inside has only failed to escape within 600 iterations: points near the boundary can escape arbitrarily late, so a higher cap could still change pixels. Agreement between two caps is evidence, not proof.

The reply says what it would take to claim more (for example detecting that an orbit has settled into a cycle, a distance estimate, or a further comparison at much higher caps), or states plainly that no finite comparison can establish it.
The reply claims no specific past experience (a render it made, an episode number) that the evidence pack does not support.

cases.title: A branching aggregate and the first membranes

cases.title: Predict Newton's fractal for z^2 - 1 without rendering

steps.say: Without rendering anything: what will Newton's fractal for z^2 - 1 look like, and what happens to a starting point on the imaginary axis? Say why this picture is so much plainer than the one for z^3 - 1.

criteria.text: The reply says that the plane splits into two half-planes: every starting point with a positive real part goes to the root 1 and every point with a negative real part goes to -1, so the picture is two plain regions.

The reply says that the boundary between them is the imaginary axis, a straight line, and that a starting point on it never converges: each Newton step keeps it on the axis, where it jumps about without settling (or lands on 0, where the step is undefined).

The reply says why it is plain: with two roots each point simply goes to the nearer root and the boundary can be a line, whereas with three roots every boundary point has to touch all three basins at once, which forces a fractal boundary.
The reply claims no specific past experience (a render it made, an episode number) that the evidence pack does not support.
